# MARKET COMMENTARY

# Gasoline cargoes

European gasoline values declined again on Wednesday, as Russia's gasoline supply deficit was reported to be shrinking.

Benchmark non-oxy barge cracks to front-month Ice Brent crude futures fell by $3.27/bl to $33.71/bl in the Tuesday session, down from $36.98/bl on Tuesday. Non-oxy cracks to Ice Brent have averaged $42.75/bl to date this month, down from $45.86/bl in September. The easing in high-octane blending component tightness from mid-September and the seasonal transition to cheaper winter-specification gasoline blends have weighed on cracks, the IEA said today in its latest Oil Market Report (OMR).

Russian gasoline import demand is falling as consumption declines seasonally and domestic supply shortfalls are being resolved, market sources said. Russia's gasoline supply gap has dropped to 250,000t/month in October from 450,000-500,000t/m in September, sources said. The shortfall was around 520,000t/m in August, they said.

Lower seasonal demand and the return of refining capacity reduced the supply gap. Deputy prime minister Alexander Novak today said several plants have resumed operations, resulting in a significantly better domestic road fuel market than recently observed. Around 1.741mn b/d in Russian crude distillation and condensate splitter capacity is offline this month, Argus Consulting estimated, which is around 1mn b/d less than the 2.852mn b/d peak in July. That month Moscow announced a diesel export ban, after a gasoline export ban in April.

Meanwhile, in Europe's top gasoline export market, US gasoline demand is forecast to fall by 2pc this year, the IEA said today in its OMR. US gasoline demand fell by 3.2pc on the year to 8.97mb b/d in August, it said. Total gasoline product supplied in the US has averaged 8.768mn b/d to date this year, according to the latest EIA data, compared to 8.79mn b/d in the same period last year.

By contrast, OECD Europe saw gasoline demand rise by 3.3pc on the year to 2.51mn b/d in August, according to the IEA. However, European sales of gasoline internal combustion engine cars (excluding non-plug-in hybrids) fell in August below 20pc for the first time, the OMR says. This was down by 7pc from year-ago levels. Diesel car sales have averaged around 6pc since the US-Iran war began.

There were no fresh price discussions reported in the non-oxy finished cargo market in northwest Europe on Wednesday. In the absence of liquidity, a $28.25/t freight differential between ARA and the Thames and an $18/t blending value were applied to indicated non-oxy barge values of $1,158/t at 16:30 BST. Non-oxy cargoes on a cif Thames basis were subsequently assessed at $1,204.25/t, and at a $41.50/t premium to the final non-oxy barge volume-weighted average (VWA).

In the Mediterranean cargo market, no fresh bid, offer or traded levels were forthcoming on Wednesday. Mediterranean cargoes were held at a premium of $176.50/t against the November Mediterranean swap, while the November Med-North spread was given at a premium of $18/t. Outright Mediterranean cargo assessments were subsequently made at $1,291.25/t and at a premium of $128.50/t to the non-oxy barge VWA, adjusted for dates and structure.

### Gasoline barges

European gasoline prices dipped in the Wednesday session, while cash premiums to underlying Eurobob oxy swaps also fell from Tuesday.

Non-oxy gasoline barges traded at a volume-weighted average (VWA) price of $1,162.75/t, down from $1,192.50/t on Tuesday. The grade was assessed at a $90/t premium to the oxy swap, down from a premium of $112/t on the session.

A total of 6,000t of non-oxy changed hands on the day, where ExxonMobil and Shell sold volumes to Varo. Trades were carried out at $1,162-1,163/t.

And 6,000t of oxy barges were reported trading at a VWA premium of $96/t to the swap, meaning outright oxy barges were assessed at a premium of $6/t to the non-oxy barge VWA, at $1,168.75/t.

In the absence of fresh indications, the 95 Ron finished-grade barge was held at premiums to non-oxy barges of $63/t, unchanged from Tuesday.

## Naphtha

European naphtha values declined on the session, as fundamentals remain unsupportive for the light end distillate.

Demand for naphtha as a petrochemical feedstock is very low because European petrochemical margins are narrow and the industry is running well below production capacity. Naphtha is one of the products dragging down margins for European refiners, as prices have not kept up with crude's rally in the last six weeks.

Naphtha averaged a $6/bl discount to North Sea Dated in August, then a $22/bl discount in September, then a $30/bl discount so far in October. European petrochemical users of naphtha have struggled economically for years, and have now found their input costs rise significantly. They have operated well below capacity this year, putting a brake on naphtha price gains.

Eurobob gasoline's premium against Dated has shrunk this autumn, but remained positive. Eurobob has averaged a premium of than $300/t against naphtha in August, September, and October so far. With naphtha so cheap in relative terms, gasoline blending economics are extremely rewarding for the time of year. But this is driving up the price of higher-octane components, needed to bring the blend up to gasoline specifications. For example, alkylate's premium against naphtha averaged nearly $900/t in September, compared with just $350/t last September.

No naphtha cargoes were reported trading in the Wednesday session. Trafigura placed the most competitive bid for a 28,000t cargo, to be delivered over 4-8 November and pricing at a discount of $5/t against balance of the month values. No offers were reported in the session. The bid normalised to $915/t, but did not challenge prevailing levels. Naphtha cargoes delivered to northwest Europe were subsequently assessed at $927.75/t on Wednesday, down by $3/t on the session, reflecting swap market levels.

## Fuel oil

Outright prices rose on the day, and margins gained ground, as new data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) show stock levels in some Asian countries have hit a record low.

HSFO refining margins have been strengthening over recent sessions. Refining discounts to front-month Ice Brent crude futures narrowed to $10.53/bl by the close of the session, drawing in from $11.61/bl by 16:30 BST on Tuesday.

Market participants said during the session that supply of HSFO in markets east of Suez is coming under pressure, as shipments coming in from Russia and the Mideast Gulf thins out, weighing on global supply levels. Europe has been relatively well-supplied with HSFO in comparison thanks to incoming shipments from South America and Syria. Kpler data show that so far in October, roughly 260,000t of higher-sulphur residual product has arrived in ARA. Around half of this total came from Mexico and Syria.

According to the latest oil market report (OMR) from the IEA released in the session, fuel oil stock levels in OECD Asia-Oceania countries have reached their lowest total on record, which go back to 1984. The countries comprise Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. Stock levels dropped to 15mn bls in August from 16.2mn bls in July.

Strength in European HSFO markets could indicate that the effects of supply tightness in Asia are now having a knock-on effect.

In the northwest European market for HSFO, BP bought 2,000t each from Vitol and Saudi Arabia state-owned Aramco Trading at between $613-615/t, all on a fob Rotterdam barge basis. Trafigura also bought 2,000t from Shell at $617/t. Fob northwest Europe HSFO barge prices were assessed at $615/t, rising from $610/t on Tuesday.

HSFO supply tightness in Europe is being slightly offset by flows coming out of Syria. So far in October, a total of 363,000t of higher-sulphur residual product has loaded in Syria, according to Kpler. In September, a total of 612,000t loaded across the month. Large volumes of Iraqi fuel oil have been shipped into Europe from the Syrian port of Banias. The Iraqi product has arrived in Syria in the first place via truck.

BP sold 4,000t of fob Rotterdam VLSFO barges to TotalEnergies at $684/t during the session. Glencore also sold 2,000t to Shell at $676/t. Fob northwest Europe barge price assessments were made at $681.25/t, based on the reported trade, rising from $671.25/t at the close of the previous session.

# NEWS

# IEA increases 2026 crude runs projection

The IEA has increased its projection for 2026 global crude runs in its latest Oil Market Report (OMR), despite predicting European crude run cuts in the fourth quarter.

The October OMR forecasts 2026 global crude throughput to fall by 2.3mn b/d on the year to 81.7mn b/d. This is 200,000 b/d higher than predicted in the September report. The OMR cited improved expectations for the return of Middle East refining and a rebound in Chinese run rates.

Despite this increased prediction for the year, European refinery throughput fell to 11.5mn b/d in September because maintenance season reduced available capacity. This was a fall of 500,000 b/d on the month. Similarly, global crude runs fell in September to 81.8mn b/d from 83mn b/d in August.

OECD throughput averaged 36.8mn b/d in September.

October is on track to be the lowest month for refinery crude throughput in the fourth quarter with the OMR anticipating an average of 81.3mn b/d globally and 10.7mn b/d in Europe. But by December this is expected to rise to 84.6mn b/d and 11.6mn b/d, respectively.

The October OMR report came with the caveat that a recent compression in European refining margins, first noted in September, "may prompt some refiners to consider economic run cuts" in the final quarter of 2026. The high prices for prompt North Sea crude grades was given as a key reason. The IEA said that most North Sea grades have increased by over $15/bl above North Sea Dated.

By Leon Wheeler

# European cracks face crude price squeeze

Rising crude prices are squeezing European refining margins, raising the possibility that refiners could cut throughput to avoid buying prompt crude or could re-sell crude they already have.

A gasoline-oriented northwest European refinery with a fluid catalytic cracker (FCC) would lose $6.50/bl on a spot WTI crude purchase on average so far in October, Argus calculates, before covering operating costs (see chart). This assumes product premiums to crude are steady to receipt of crude. Simple refineries with no FCC nor other cracking units would lose around $19/bl on a spot WTI crude purchase this week, before covering costs.

Standard costs come to $5-10/bl.

A refinery with a hydrocracker could make around $13/bl before costs because these units maximise production of diesel and jet fuel, which are the highest-priced products at present. But margins are trending down even for hydrocracker-equipped refineries, having averaged $38/bl before costs in September.

Delivered crude prices in Europe increased in October as global tanker freight costs rose after attacks on shipping in the Middle East and the Black Sea. A Panamax tanker carrying crude from the US to Europe cost $200/t or $27/bl in the second week of October, four times more than in the second week of September.

Crude prices had already risen in September, resulting from the closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and a slowdown in releases from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). Saudi Arabia has exported around 2.5mn b/d from its Red Sea port of Yanbu in September and October, according to Vortexa, down from above 4mn b/d earlier this year. US SPR releases have been below 200,000 b/d since September, after 1mn-1.5mn b/d in the second quarter.

The effect of this on northwest European refiners is broadly dependent on configuration. Argus research finds 14 of the 80 standard refineries in Europe have an FCC but no hydrocracker, nor a coker unit that boosts middle distillate output. Nine of those 14 are in northern Europe. Two are by the Mediterranean and three are fed by pipelines from Mediterranean ports.

If FCC-oriented refineries were to cut throughput, northern European crude and product markets would be most strongly affected. There are few simple refineries in Europe, which have struggled to be profitable even under more stable conditions.

European refiners are struggling to pass on the cost of crude to buyers of products other than diesel and jet fuel. Demand for naphtha as a petrochemical feedstock is very low, because European petrochemical margins are narrow and the industry is running well below production capacity. Gasoline prices have rallied as refiners prioritise diesel and jet fuel, but neither the US-Iran war nor the Russia-Ukraine war directly affects gasoline supply as much as diesel and jet fuel.

The drop in refinery margins is not as deep as one in April, around a month into the effective closure of the strait of Hormuz and before the US SPR releases began. Even refineries with hydrocrackers looked loss-making after costs in the second week of April, and those with FCCs were in a similar position for the first three weeks of that month.

European crude receipts at EU and UK ports have averaged around 10.7mn b/d in 2026, according to Vortexa, up from around 10.6mn b/d in the same period of 2025. Huge stock draws in the US and China have helped sustain global refinery runs.

By Benedict George, Michael Carolan and Ellanee Kruck

## Global diesel tightness to stretch into 2027: IEA

Supplies of diesel and gasoil will not match demand in the fourth quarter of this year, making it unlikely that inventories will be rebuilt to normal levels before the second half of 2027, the IEA said in its latest Oil Market Report (OMR).

Inventories have dropped because of constraints to supply outpacing higher prices slowing demand. Total OECD stocks of diesel and gasoil fell to their lowest since November 2023 at 565mn bl in July, down by 5pc compared with before the war in the Middle East, the IEA said.

The agency estimates the global balance of diesel and other gasoil — supply minus demand, which gives an implied stock change — tightened by roughly 100,000 b/d in the third quarter. Normally stocks build during the third quarter — in the third quarter of 2025 they increased by 880,000 b/d, while the average build over the past five years was 300,000 b/d.

The IEA predicts that the stockdraw will speed up in October as global demand rises and refineries conduct maintenance. Rising crude and freight prices have weighed on refinery margins outside North America. Further drops in refinery margins could drive run cuts, pressuring supply more, the agency said.

The loosening of Russia's diesel export ban should not materially boost supply because of currently reduced Russian refinery capacity, according to the IEA.

Stocks should build seasonally in the first quarter of 2027 as global refinery runs pick up, but that will not be enough to offset draws seen this year, the IEA said, adding that recovery depends on the return of Middle East supplies. Without the Middle East stepping up, the IEA suggested that more demand loss could be required to balance the market. Government intervention to limit road fuel prices stymied demand loss across the summer in Europe.

The IEA estimated that global production of diesel and gasoil fell by 1.7mn b/d on the year to 27.2mn b/d in the third quarter, more sharply than the 1.5mn b/d drop in the second quarter. Alongside reduced output from the Middle East and Russia, shifted yields towards jet fuel weighed on diesel supply, as did refineries using crude not ideal for their configurations.

That lower output pushed global exports of diesel and gasoil down by 10pc on the year in January-September to 4.7mn b/d, according to the IEA. Exports fell particularly steeply in September, by 700,000 b/d on the year to 4.7mn b/d, as higher volumes from the US and China failed to offset the gap created by the Middle East and Russia.

Extremely high prices and weaker forecasts of economic activity have weighed on global demand for diesel and gasoil, but not enough to match the loss of supply, the IEA said. Deliveries of diesel and gasoil fell by 750,000 b/d on the year to 28.7mn b/d in the third quarter.

Heating oil demand has fallen markedly since the start of the war, particularly as consumers delayed their normal restocking over summer. Deliveries of non-transport gasoil in OECD counties fell by 8pc on the year in March-July, while deliveries of diesel fell by only 2pc, the IEA said. Heating oil consumers will have to restock ahead of winter, but the IEA forecast that global demand for diesel and other gasoil will still fall by 1mn b/d in the fourth quarter.

By Josh Michalowski

## Russian gasoline import demand falling: Sources

Russian gasoline import demand is falling as consumption declines seasonally and domestic supply shortfalls are being resolved, market sources said.

Russia's gasoline supply gap has dropped to 250,000t in October from 450,000-500,000t in September, sources said. The shortfall was around 520,000t in August, they said.

Lower seasonal demand and the return of refining capacity reduced the supply gap. Deputy prime minister Alexander Novak today said several plants have resumed operations, resulting in a significantly better domestic road fuel market than recently observed.

Around 1.741mn b/d in Russian crude distillation and condensate splitter capacity is offline this month, Argus Consulting estimated, which is around 1mn b/d less than the 2.852mn b/d peak in July. That month Moscow announced a diesel export ban, after a gasoline export ban in April.

Russian sources anticipate the privately owned Surgut-neftegaz's 350,000 b/d Kirishi refinery will restart by the end of this month, which could balance the domestic gasoline market from November, provided there are no new Ukrainian attacks on refineries.

The most recent attack was on Gazpromneft's 430,000 b/d Omsk refinery — one of Russia's largest gasoline-producing facilities — on 9 October. It is unclear if the energy ceasefire announced by US president Donald Trump on 11 October will lead to a sustained reduction in Ukrainian drone strikes.

Gasoline exports for Russian delivery peaked in August, when 87,000 b/d was loaded from Morocco, Turkey and South Korea, Kpler data show. Loadings fell to 9,000 b/d in September and are 22,000 b/d this month.

This declining Russian import demand is probably dampening interest for Mediterranean supply, with fob Mediterranean gasoline cargo premiums to benchmark non-oxy barges falling from a record $100.75/t in September to an average of $92.75/t in October.

Russia's shift from exporter to importer in August was clearly removing supply from the global pool, a gasoline analyst said at the time.

By George Maher-Bonnett

### Asia-Pac OECD fuel oil stocks at record low: IEA

Asia-Pacific OECD countries' fuel oil stocks have fallen to their lowest on record, according to the IEA, as cargo flows to the region remain thin on the back of attacks on shipping.

Total industry stocks of fuel oil held by OECD countries in Asia-Pacific fell to an all-time low in August, according to the agency's latest oil market report (OMR), released today, dropping to 15mn bl from 16.2mn bl in July. IEA records go back to 1984, and the only countries included in Asia-Pacific are Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand.

Participants active in the fuel oil market said today that overall levels in Asia are very tight, especially HSFO.

HSFO supply to customers east of Suez has been heavily disrupted by the continued risk to ships transiting the strait of Hormuz, as well as leaving Black sea ports.

Disruption to very-low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) imports has led buyers in Asia to take in product from more unusual sources. Japan imported low-sulphur product from Argentina in September, for the first time since at least 2017.

By Bob Wigin

### Lufthansa buys minority stake in Portugal's TAP

The Portuguese government today selected a bid from Germany's Lufthansa Group to buy a minority stake in flag carrier TAP Air Portugal, for an initial price of $1.025bn.

Lisbon gave the green light for Lufthansa to acquire 44.9pc of TAP, which could rise to 49.9pc for an extra $175mn, if TAP employees do not exercise their right to purchase a combined 5pc of the shares. The Portuguese state remains the majority shareholder, via its holding company Parpublica.

Lufthansa's bid was 16pc higher than the rival bid from Air France-KLM, Portuguese prime minister Luis Montenegro said.

Lufthansa is now finalising the transaction with the Portuguese government and Parpublica. The group's chief executive, Carsten Spohr, said that TAP strengthens Lufthansa's position in the South Atlantic, namely in Latin America.

TAP's net profit was €4mn in 2025, down from €54mn the year before. It carried 16.7mn passengers in 2025.

The Lufthansa Group is the parent company of Lufthansa Airlines, Swiss, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines and Eurowings. The group's net profit was €1.34bn in 2025.

The TAP acquisition marks further consolidation of airlines in the European market. Airlines owned by Lufthansa, Air France-KLM and IAG operated a combined average of 7,585 flights per day across the Eurocontrol network during 21-27 September, over 20pc of total flights in the 42 states that Eurocontrol monitors over that period.

By Amaar Khan

### Hormuz disruptions reshape shipping: SIBCON

Geopolitical tensions are altering cargo movements, voyage patterns and bunker demand across global shipping markets, forcing shipowners and fuel suppliers to adapt to rising costs, shifting trade routes and growing uncertainty, industry executives said at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference and Exhibition (SIBCON) 2026.

Recent disruptions in the strait of Hormuz have reinforced the need for a broader range of marine fuel options, including LNG, methanol, ammonia and biofuels, both to support decarbonisation efforts and reduce exposure to supply shocks affecting conventional fuels.

But participants warned that fragmented regional regulations including the EU emissions trading system (ETS) and FuelEU Maritime rules alongside separate IMO requirements are complicating investment decisions at a time when shipowners must commit capital to vessels expected to trade for 20-25 years. Uncertainty over future compliance costs, fuel availability and bunkering infrastructure remain a key hurdle to wider adoption of alternative-fuel vessels.

While much of the discussion centred on shipping's energy transition, panellists agreed that geopolitical developments will continue to influence global shipping markets, with supply chain disruptions increasingly shaping vessel deployment, trading patterns and operating costs across sectors.

# Gibraltar bunkering calls rise in Sep

The Mediterranean port of Gibraltar recorded 477 bunkering calls in September, up from 431 a year earlier and 476 in August, according to the Gibraltar Port Authority (GPA).

Bunker fuel prices in Gibraltar rose in September in line with the broader European trend. Very-low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) values rose by 6.2pc and marine gasoil (MGO) by 13pc, as tight prompt availability supported higher prices.

Resilient demand reflects Gibraltar's position — along with Spain's Algeciras and Ceuta — as the final opportunity for ship operators to bunker with low-sulphur fuel before entering the Mediterranean emission control area (ECA), where vessels must use fuel containing up to 0.1pc sulphur.

Gibraltar is typically cheaper than other regional ports. On 14 October, Argus assessed Gibraltar VLSFO at $728.50/t and MGO at $1,505/t, compared with $832.50/t and $1,537.50/t, respectively, in Piraeus, Greece.

By Natália Coelho

### Change to Eurobob gasoline assessments: Update

Argus has observed that bids, offers and trade in the Eurobob gasoline market remain discussed as a differential to the underlying Eurobob oxy gasoline swap and have not transitioned to refer to the increasingly liquid trade in Eurobob non-oxy gasoline swaps. As a result, Argus will assess Eurobob oxy and non-oxy barge markets based on their differentials to whatever floating price reference is commonly used by the market, rather than solely against the Eurobob non-oxy swap price as previously stated.

Should Eurobob oxy and non-oxy barges trade at differentials to different underlying derivatives prices, Argus will standardise that market information to a common differential basis. The common differential basis will be the one used for the larger share of physical Eurobob non-oxy barge trades on the day of assessment.

Argus will revisit this aspect of the Eurobob methodology should market conditions change.

Following industry consultation and effective 1 January 2024, Argus will assess the Eurobob oxy gasoline barge price as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy barge price. There has been strong support from market participants for the change because E10 is now the primary grade in the northwest European gasoline market.

In addition, from 1 January 2024, Argus will use bids, offers and trades for Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges that are expressed as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy futures price to assess the price of both gasoline grades.

### Continuation of Argus Eurobob oxy assessment

Following requests from market participants, Argus confirms previous guidance that it will continue to publish the Eurobob oxy barge assessment and that it has no plans to discontinue the assessment. Argus notes strong interest from market participants to continue to actively trade both Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges.

### New Eurobob oxy methodology from 1 January 2024

From 1 January 2024, the Eurobob oxy price will be constructed as follows:

- Volume weighted averages of the differentials at which Eurobob oxy and Eurobob non-oxy barges have traded against the common floating Eurobob derivative price will be calculated;
- Then the difference between those volume-weighted averages will be subtracted from the final Eurobob non-oxy price assessment for that day to arrive at the Eurobob oxy barge price assessment;
- The common differential basis will be the one used for the larger share of physical Eurobob non-oxy barge trades on the day of assessment.

### Eurobob non-oxy derivatives are already available for trade

A full range of financial derivatives referencing Argus Eurobob non-oxy gasoline barge assessments are already listed on futures exchanges, and these assessments have been part of Argus' annual assurance review under the IOSCO principles since 2019.

### Eurobob oxy prices to continue beyond the end of 2024

- Argus will continue to publish the Eurobob oxy barge price beyond 31 December 2024, assessed as a differential to the Eurobob non-oxy barge price as described above.
- A legacy volume-weighted-average price for Eurobob oxy barges, calculated as the volume-weighted average of the outright $/t prices of Eurobob oxy barge trades, will be published after 1 January 2024, but with a new Argus code.

### Clarification of European Russian-origin product restrictions

For the avoidance of doubt, beginning with prices assessed on 22 December, for all European product prices, except those under the header "Russian refined products", Argus will align its definition of Russian origin with that of EU (and/or UK, where applicable) sanctions regulation. On 22 December, Argus will simplify its previous definitions of non-Russian origin in the Argus European Products methodology, which will be replaced with "compliant with all EU sanctions in force or scheduled to be in force on 21 January 2026, including but not limited to Article 3ma of council regulation 833/2014".

Please contact benedict.george@argusmedia.com with any questions.

# Argus successfully completes annual losco assurance review

Argus has completed the 13th external assurance review of its price benchmarks covering crude oil, oil products, LPG, chemicals, thermal and coking coal, natural gas, biofuels, biomass, metals, fertilizers and agricultural markets. The review was carried out by professional services firm PwC. Annual independent, external reviews of oil benchmarks are required by international regulatory group losco's Principles for Oil Price Reporting Agencies, and losco encourages extension of the reviews to non-oil benchmarks. For more information and to download the review visit our website www.argusmedia.com/en/about-us/governance-compliance

# Eurobob gasoline seasonal transition dates

Argus Eurobob gasoline barge price assessments will be based only on information about trade in winter grades until 23 March 2026, and based only on summer grades from 27 March 2026 until 22 September 2026. The assessments will be based only on winter grades from 28 September 2026.

During the 24-26 March and 23-25 September seasonal transition periods, at least 3,000t of summer-specification trade and 3,000t of winter-specification trade are required to calculate the volume-weighted average. If less than 3,000t of trade of either grade within Argus' criteria is reported, Argus will include in the volume-weighted average an assessment of the prevailing market price for the relevant grade at 4:30pm London time. That assessment will be assigned whatever volume is required such that the total volume of reported trades and the assessment for that grade equals 3,000t.

# Subscriber notice: Gasoline barges

For trades to be included in Argus gasoline barge assessments, standard nomination procedures must be followed. The buyer should give two working days' notice of barge ETA. Nominations received after 14:00 London time or on Fridays after 13:00 London time will be deemed to be received on the following working day. Otherwise, the original day of nomination will count as day one of the two days notice.

Quality testing: On gasoline barges, standard industry practice assumes seller's discretion to appoint an inspections company from a list of widely recognised entities. But if a buyer has reasonable cause* to request an alternative but widely recognised inspector, the nominated inspection company should be changed by mutual agreement. If changing the nominated inspection company is not acceptable to the seller, the seller should agree to allow a re-test of the product by an alternative inspections company before loading.
*Reasonable cause may include recent history of deviations between test results at loadport and/or on delivery, where the deviation is in excess of industry accepted margins of reproducibility and repeatability.

# Using EU ETS-inclusive WS tanker rates

Following consultation, Argus tanker rates will use the version of flat rates published by the Worldscale Association that include EU emissions trading system (ETS) costs.

Argus Tanker Freight will continue to publish a selection of ETS costs for tankers as Carbon Costs of Freight (CCFs).

To discuss this announcement, please contact freightteam@argusmedia.com
